content: The Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) is a non-governmental, non-profit organization that receives funding from companies with vested interests in cancer-related initiatives. Dr. Lynette Denny has delivered presentations on HPV vaccination at forums organized by GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) and Merck. For these activities, honoraria of approximately $4,000 per company per year were paid to her employer, the University of Cape Town. Additionally, the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at the University of Cape Town, under Dr. Denny's leadership, has conducted two HPV vaccine trials for GSK and Merck. GSK provided $6 million in funding, while Merck's funding was directed to the Department of Health in KwaZulu-Natal. Dr. Denny's contributions to these projects were pro bono. In 2012, she gave a talk in Hong Kong on the cost-effectiveness of HPV testing, with travel, registration, and accommodation expenses covered by Qiagen. Currently, she is leading a trial for Roche to evaluate the cobas® 4800 System's cancer detection capabilities, with a project cost of $25,000. All funds received by Dr. Denny, whether as a principal investigator or speaker, are allocated to the University of Cape Town's research accounts. Dr. Silvia de Sanjosé has occasionally received travel support from Sanofi, Merck, and Qiagen to attend and present study results at national and international conferences. These trips were funded in amounts ranging from $1,000 to $3,000, depending on the conference location. None of the funders influenced the presentation of results, data collection, analysis, or interpretation. Dr. Eduardo Franco has participated in advisory board meetings and forums on cervical cancer prevention strategies organized by Merck, Roche, and Gen-Probe, focusing on HPV vaccines and tests. He has received an average honorarium of $4,000 per company annually over the past four years. Dr. Julia Gage, as part of her work with the U.S. National Cancer Institute (NCI), conducted an operations research project in Nigeria to evaluate the careHPV screening test developed by Qiagen. Qiagen donated reagents, equipment, and supplies, while NCI covered all other study expenses. Dr. Francisco Garcia, during his tenure at the University of Arizona, served as the principal investigator for drug trials involving novel agents for cervical cancer treatment. These trials were conducted under research contracts with Roche ($150,000), Inovio ($70,000), Photocure ($120,000), and Roche/Ventana ($100,000). Dr. Garcia did not receive personal income from these trials. Dr. José Jeronimo is an employee of PATH, an international non-profit organization focused on developing and delivering cost-effective global health tools. PATH has collaborated with Qiagen and Arbor Vita to develop rapid HPV tests and cervical cancer screening tools. These tests are prioritized for commercialization in China and India and will be made available at low cost to public sectors in low-resource countries. Dr. Enriquito Lu was the principal investigator for an HPV vaccination study conducted by Jhpiego, an international non-profit organization, under an agreement with Merck. The study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of integrating HPV vaccination for girls aged 9–13 into cervical cancer prevention programs for mothers in Thailand and the Philippines. Merck provided $850,000 and HPV vaccines for up to 4,000 girls at each project site. Dr. Lu did not receive personal income for his work on this study. Dr. Raul Murillo served as a consultant for GSK to analyze the cost-effectiveness of the HPV vaccine. Dr. Swee Chong Quek has participated in advisory board meetings and forums organized by GSK and Qiagen over the past four years. These activities focused on cervical cancer prevention strategies, HPV vaccine efficacy studies, and the clinical relevance of HPV vaccination. Dr. Quek received a total income of S$9,000 (Singapore dollars) for these activities. Dr. Achim Schneider serves as an advisor to Karl Storz, assisting in the development of laparoscopic techniques and instruments for treating cervical cancer and other diseases. He receives an annual honorarium of €40,000. Additionally, he has participated in advisory board meetings and lectures on HPV vaccination organized by GSK and Sanofi, for which he received a combined income of $20,000 over the past four years. Dr. Vivien Tsu, an employee of PATH, has been involved in large-scale demonstration projects on cervical cancer prevention, screening, and treatment in developing countries. PATH received donated vaccines from GSK and Merck and careHPV tests from Qiagen for these projects. Dr. Tsu also participated in an alternative-dose-schedule study in Vietnam, supported by donated vaccines from Merck. The WHO guidelines for screening and treating precancerous cervical lesions provide decision-making flowcharts to assist program managers in selecting appropriate screen-and-treat strategies. These flowcharts consider factors such as resource availability, costs, staff training, and follow-up rates. Specific strategies include HPV testing followed by visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) or colposcopy, with treatment options such as cryotherapy or loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP). Recommendations vary based on HIV status and resource settings, with detailed guidance provided in the guidelines' annexes and supplemental materials.
